en: Table of Contents for the Forty-Eight Questions on the Precept Against Killing:
Explanation of the Doubt Concerning Living Beings Sustaining Humans (Five Questions); Explanation of the Doubt Concerning the Secular View that Killing Should Be Abandoned (Six Questions);

Explanation of the Doubt Concerning the Difficulty of Saving Those with Heavy Karmic Retribution (Five Questions); Explanation of the Doubt Concerning the Use of Strong-smelling Foods and Blood in Praying to the Gods (Three Questions).
Resolving Doubts Regarding Sacrificing to Ancestors (Four Questions); Resolving Doubts Regarding Feasting Guests in Contravention of Custom (One Question);
Resolving Doubts Regarding the Ancient Sages’ Teachings on Killing (Two Questions); Resolving Doubts Regarding Benevolence toward the People and Compassion for All Things (Two Questions);
Resolving Doubts Regarding the Distinctions of Cause and Effect (Six Questions); Resolving Doubts Regarding the Existence or Non-existence of Evil Karma (Four Questions).

Resolving Doubts Regarding the Observance of the Fasting Precepts and the Abstinence from Meat (Seven Questions); Resolving Doubts Regarding the Difficulty of Believing the Buddha’s Teachings (Three Questions);
Forty-Eight Questions on the Prohibition of Killing (Including Preface).
Composed by Zhou Sirén of Kūnshān.
Alas! The arrival of the kalpa of slaughter is indeed a tragedy. Within the human realm, one may encounter it only once every few decades or even more than a hundred years;
yet within the realm of animals, there is not a day one does not encounter it—every time a cock crows.
There are then limitless, heartless butchers who, grasping sharp blades, suddenly bind and restrain the herd of animals.
Knowing they cannot escape, the animals leap about with loud cries that shake the earth and startle the heavens. As no rescue arrives, each is torn apart by human-faced rākṣasas;
their entrails are pulled out and their lungs extracted. Before their wailing has ceased, they are cast again into boiling water, where they undergo great suffering.
In a moment of agony, hundreds of millions of living beings had their bodies and heads severed from one another. Alas!
Did he alone not fear being killed? Bound by others, he died in bitter indignation; his grievance could not be redressed, and it festered into a malevolent qi.
When malevolent forces gather together, the heavenly devas and māras consequently appear in the world to resolve this case.
As the Chan Master Cishou said in a verse: "In the world, there is much killing of living beings; thus, the kalpa of weapons arises. Those who have taken life shall kill your own body."
"Lack of wealth shall burn your house; you shall be separated from your wife and children. Because you once destroyed another's nest, the retribution is exactly proportionate.
Wash your ears and listen to the Buddha’s teaching. Viewed from this perspective, the arrival of the kalpa of slaughter is summoned by the karmic deeds of killing committed by every individual.
Therefore, for those facing the kalpa of slaughter who contemplate how to escape it, they must rely solely on the precepts."
It turns [the cycle] around; its mechanism is most swift, its resonance most divine, and no other good deed can surpass it.
Therefore, I have composed one scroll of "Questions and Answers on Refraining from Killing" to resolve people's doubts and strengthen their faith.

My wish is that all sentient beings of this great earth may, regarding past karmic offenses of killing, transcend them through the recitation of the Buddha's name, and regarding future karmic offenses of killing, sever them immediately.
I exclude this. I shall give rise to great compassion and great fortitude, vowing never to intentionally kill even a single minute living being.
Even so, I still fear that I may not escape the calamity of killing. Let the eight classes of Vajrapāṇis cut off my head and depart!
Resolving the Doubt that Living Beings Exist for the Sustenance of Humans (The Fifth Question).
A guest said: "The Book says, 'Heaven and Earth are the parents of the myriad things; man is the spirit of the myriad things.
Heaven produced diverse species fundamentally for the purpose of sustaining humans. Why, then, is it forbidden to kill them?"
The answer is: Since one knows that Heaven and Earth are the parents of all things, one should know that all things are the infants of Heaven and Earth.
Within these infants, there are those who use strength to oppress the weak and the noble to deceive the humble; even the parents find this deeply displeasing.
If one were to claim that Heaven nourishes me by providing this flesh for consumption, then since tigers, leopards, mosquitoes, and gadflies also feed on the blood and flesh of human beings,
would it follow that Heaven created humans merely to serve as food for mosquitoes, gadflies, tigers, and leopards?
The guest asked, "If that is so, why does Heaven not manifest its retribution to prohibit people from killing?
He replied, "Heaven certainly prohibits it; therefore, it repeatedly manifests the retribution for killing. It is only the foolish who, being unaware, tread upon it;
the wise know of it yet deliberately tread upon it. Heaven can do nothing about this."

(A certain year during the Xianfeng era. A resident of Quanpao County was sleeping at night when he dreamed that a deity warned him, saying: "The soldiers will arrive within days; if you do not cease from killing, it will be difficult to escape death. Chen woke up in alarm and led his entire family, great and small, to burn incense and take an oath to forever sever their karmic habit of killing.

Everyone followed his lead, except for one woman who said, "This is merely a dream; why should it be believed? Not many days later, the soldiers arrived. The rest of the family fled, but this woman, because she was attached to her home, left slightly later and was subsequently killed.
I personally witnessed this—recorded as a postscript by the Layman Lianxi).

The guest said, "The world contains a vast multitude of species. If every person were to refrain from killing, life would continue to proliferate without end until it becomes a world of birds and beasts. What is to be done?"
The answer is: Earthworms, insects, and snakes are things that people do not eat; yet have you ever seen them filling the world?

How much more so regarding the abundance of birds and beasts in the world, which exists precisely because there are many who kill them. When grievances are requited one another, beings mutually become animals, thereby forming a world of birds and beasts.
If every person were to observe the precept against killing, then the karmic retribution of these various species would gradually [diminish].
It will surely vanish. Furthermore, the number of humans and devas will increase. When the state of Chu did not catch frogs, the frogs instead became scarce;
when Shu did not eat crabs, the crabs naturally grew rare. Is this not clear evidence?
The guest said: "If Heaven already abhors killing, it should cause the taste of blood and flesh to become foul and unbearable;
then, throughout the world, people would naturally refrain from killing—is this not excellent?"
The answer is: The flesh and blood of birds and beasts, viewed from the perspective of the heavens, are fundamentally foul-smelling and unbearable.

That people of the world eat them and perceive them as delicious is like a dung-worm that craves excrement; through habituation, they fail to realize its true nature. It is like someone who, having been a cat in a previous life, was constantly intent on catching mice;
or having been a crane in a previous life, was constantly intent on swallowing snakes; even when born as a human in this present life, [they still harbor those tendencies].
He further reflected on these two things: one is the physical form, and the other is craving. Since their cravings differ, they arise from karmic conditions;

since those karmic conditions differ, they also arise from the mind. A human being can share the same mind as a celestial being, yet one realizes for oneself that the taste of blood and flesh is foul and unbearable.
The guest said: "Those who take killing as their occupation rely upon it for supporting those above and sustaining those below.
To exhort them to change their profession is to cut off their means of livelihood. I do not approve of loving things while failing to love people."
The answer is: To take the taking of life as one’s occupation is like eating rotten meat to stave off hunger;

though one may temporarily obtain food and clothing, one will suffer through kalpas without end. It is precisely because of their attachment that they are urged to change their occupation, yet they instead claim this cuts off their livelihood.
Have those in the world who do not take the taking of life as their occupation ever died? They simply fail to reflect.
Resolving Laypeople’s Doubts Regarding the Severance of Life (Question Six):
A guest said, "Oxen can plow fields and dogs can guard at night; they truly deserve compassion. But pigs and sheep are capable of nothing;
if one does not eat them, what use are they?"
The answer is: Abstaining from killing and releasing living beings is nothing more than preserving one’s own sense of compassion;
how could it depend on whether a creature is useful or useless? To refrain from eating because of utility is still an expression of self-centeredness.
How profound is the obscuration of one's nature by habit! How love arises from greed!
The guest said: "Chickens, dogs, oxen, and sheep all cry out in grief and fear death; it is truly unbearable to kill them.
But as for minute aquatic creatures, which shed neither sound nor tears when killed—what need is there for a precept regarding them?"
The answer is: Form has magnitude and smallness, but nature has neither magnitude nor smallness. For example, if one kills a person, whether it be an elder or an infant, the offense is the same.
If you claim that killing one who makes no sound or sheds no tears does not cause pain, try observing this when a mute person is being executed.
The guest said, "To take up a knife and cut oneself is certainly harmful to a compassionate heart; but if someone else kills it and I eat it, what is there that is improper?

He replied, "This is like the proverb of 'plugging one's ears while stealing a bell. If you claim that because someone else killed it, you may shift the blame onto that person, [you have failed to understand the nature of karma]."
Thus, those who are subjected to official punishment should only resent their jailers; they should not resent their superiors. Alas!
If one can be deceived by external things, can one’s own mind be deceived?
The guest said, "Releasing living beings is certainly a virtuous deed; however, what can be done if the creatures released are subsequently captured by others?

He replied, "The captor captures on his own account, and the releaser releases on his own account. It is like a skilled physician treating an illness: he cannot guarantee that the patient will not die in the future.
It is like providing gruel during a year of famine: one cannot guarantee that people will not go hungry again the following day. Worldly...
All matters are like this; why do you alone harbor doubts regarding the release of living beings?
Furthermore, how can you know for certain that every single creature released has not been recaptured by others, so that not one survives?
The guest said, "In practicing goodness, the primary thing is to establish one's intention. If the mind is indeed good, why is it necessary to observe the precept against killing?
I replied, "Why do you say this? That which you call a 'good mind' is for the sake of the pleasure of the palate, causing all classes of living beings to endure suffering as vast as the heavens.
Among the wicked and poisonous minds in the world, none is more extreme than this. Let us test this so-called 'good mind': where else does it reside?"
[This concerns] the locus [of humanity]. Mencius said: "A human being is one who possesses benevolence (*ren*). To be benevolent is to refrain from killing; to kill is to be unbenevolent.
Throughout the world, there is absolutely no benevolent person who delights in killing."
The guest said, "I am neither for nor against; I do not prohibit killing, nor do I fail to prohibit it.
I simply set it aside with no mind.
The reply was, "To prohibit it without a mind will likely be of no merit; yet how can one avoid guilt by killing without a mind? It is like this:"
"Bandits and thieves plundered another's house; a flying arrow by mistake struck you. Can you forgive them for their lack of intent?
(The fifth question regarding the doubt that karmic retribution is heavy and difficult to escape.
The guest said: "When things are butchered and cut up, the guilt is difficult to evade. Even if I do not kill, there will surely be someone who kills."
"What harm is there in killing them?
He replied, "If the transgressions of other beings cannot be escaped, can one's own transgressions alone be escaped?
To kill another because their transgressions cannot be escaped is to share in that same unavoidable transgression. It is a principle that they devour and kill one another."
This is inevitable. How can a person remain in a place where escape is impossible without considering how to flee early on?
The guest said: "The lives of beings in this world are mostly like debts; what crime is there in killing them?"

The answer is: It is indeed true that one repays debts through the lives of sentient beings; however, there is simply a distinction between those who experience the retribution for killing face-to-face and those who do not.
As for those who experience the retribution for killing face-to-face, it is because in a previous life they once killed me, and now we have encountered one another as karmic enemies.

It is only right that I should receive retribution from them. As for those who did not face me when they received the fruit of their own killing—others in previous lives who were once killed by me—even though the karmic retribution has now reached me, it is not appropriate that I should pay it back to them.
In the space of a single banquet among the people of the world, there are several kinds of meat offerings; yet within a single slice of meat, there are hundreds of thousands of minute lives.
How could one possibly take all of them as those who face one to receive retribution and kill them? I fear that such taking [of life] will lead to consequences.
Regarding those who settle their debts in a previous life, one might rarely find even one or two such cases; yet those who incur debts for their future lives are as numerous as they are common.
A guest said: "If one kills without facing the recipient of the harm, there will certainly be retribution. But if one faces the recipient, [the matter is] one way and then another..."
"Come! Once the retribution for killing is exhausted, what harm is there?
He replied: "Do you not see people in the marketplace fighting one another? This person comes with a staff, and that person goes forth with a staff;
their fists descend upon each other like rain. Have you ever seen them, after this coming and going, each withdraw their hands and settle their minds in equanimity? Bodhi—
Regarding causes and conditions in the future, he perceives them as clearly as looking at fire; this is why, even when encountering enemies, he does not seek retribution.
A guest asked: "The Buddha said that among those born into existence, many have been one's parents or six types of relatives in past lives.
What evidence is there for such a statement?"
The answer is: Sentient beings of the six realms have been wandering in saṃsāra without ceasing for immeasurable kalpas. Even considering just a single kalpa, their number is infinite.
How can one fail to see that among the living beings before our eyes, there are none who are not related to us? I once saw Liu Daoyuan serving as the magistrate of Pengxi;
upon his retirement from office, he stayed overnight at the home of the Qin family. He dreamed of a woman weeping and saying, "I am..."

She was the wife of Qin. Because she had caused a maidservant to be buried alive in an earthen mound, the officials of the underworld sentenced her to death and further punished her by transforming her into a sheep.
She is currently in the pen; tomorrow, she will be slaughtered to serve as an offering for you. Liu hurriedly informed him, but it was already too late to save her.
The entire family wailed in great sorrow. Alas! There are many such cases in the world; it is simply that those with the "fleshly eye" do not perceive them. How tragic!

(In the third year of the Xianfeng era, there was a son of the Li family in Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, who committed every kind of evil. In his present life, he transformed into a pig. His family sent him to a subordinate monastery at Yunqi for release.
He was personally seen by the Grand Secretary Xu Yinting. Recorded as a supplement by the Layman Lianxi.)

The guest said: "When I see people killing living beings, or those catching fish and birds, although I give rise to the vow to rescue and deliver them, my power does not follow my heart's intent. What can be done?"

The answer is: If one sees someone killing a living being, they should silently maintain all divine mantras or recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, and on behalf of the creature, give rise to a mind of repentance;
then the creature being killed will naturally receive benefit. If one sees someone catching fish or birds...
Focus your attention on that person and do not give rise to other thoughts. Silently recite "Namo to the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna" several dozen times.
Fish and birds alike may escape their nets. (This method has been tested repeatedly and proven effective; by all means, do not treat it with negligence.)
Resolving Doubts Regarding Sacrifices of Meat and Blood to Pray to the Spirits (Part Three, Question One).
A guest said: "Those who pray to the spirits do so either to seek the birth of a son or the extension of their lifespan, or to seek fame, office, wealth, and goods.
If one abandons the sacrificial victims, how can one manifest reverence? What is to be done?"
The answer is: Heaven, earth, and the spiritual deities cherish life and loathe killing.

To cause creatures to lose their offspring while seeking them, to diminish one’s lifespan while seeking longevity, or to sacrifice one’s life for fame and profit—this is not only intolerable by the principles of heaven, but even one’s own heart cannot bear it.
It is not merely useless; it further brings harm.
The guest said, "Generally, those who observe the fast may use vegetarian offerings for sacrifices. However, if one comes from a family that eats meat, it is a profound insult to the deities.

I replied, "The *I Ching* says: 'The ox slaughtered by the neighbor to the east is not as good as the simple summer sacrifice of the neighbor to the west; yet the latter truly receives its blessing.'"
The Records say: "The vegetation of mountain torrents, streams, ponds, and marshes—the pondweed, duckweed, water-moss, and water-weed—may be offered to the ghosts and spirits.
How could the spirits in heaven compete with humans for meat?"
The guest asked, "Is it true that spirits who subsist on blood offerings can also fall into hell?
He replied, "In past lives, they were upright and thus became deities. Among those who are upright, those whose compassionate hearts prevail do not receive blood offerings;
among those who are upright, those whose anger prevails must receive blood offerings. For those whose compassion prevails, their wisdom is superior..."
If merit is full, one will not sink into the depths of samsara. If the mind of anger prevails, merit may surpass wisdom, yet when its retribution is exhausted, one cannot avoid falling.
One should know that Heaven loves life; it is not only humans who ought to embody this principle.
Resolving Doubts Regarding Sacrificing to Ancestors (Four Questions).

A guest said: "I certainly know that it is improper to kill living beings for the sake of sacrificing to deities; however, I do not know whether there is also sin in killing living beings for the sake of nourishing one's parents."
The answer is: It is even worse than that. The *Li* (Book of Rites) says: "To attribute virtue to one's parents and to attribute faults to oneself is the way of a filial son.
If you yourself do not kill, yet kill solely for the sake of nourishing your parents, this is to attribute the fault to your parents.

Can you bear this in your heart? If it is unavoidable, one may use the three kinds of pure meat (*tri-śuddha-māṃsa*: not seen being killed, not heard being killed, and not suspected to have been killed for one's sake), as well as... [self-]killed [meat].
"Offer dead meat. This may be a way to achieve both ends.

The guest said, "In a filial son’s repayment of his origins, nothing is more important than the ancestral sacrifice. If one's parents did not observe the fast during their lives, yet one uses vegetarian offerings after their death, it is not in accord with filial piety toward one's kin."
The answer is: If one claims that ancestors are satiated by means of sacrifices, then since sacrifices are performed no more than a few times in a year, they would surely suffer from hunger.
On the other hand, if one claims that whether they are hungry or not does not depend on this, then sacrifice is merely a matter of the filial son’s heart.
How could it be considered "exhausting one's heart" to engage in the act of slaughtering and creating karma? Furthermore, even when a filial son nourishes his parents, he still requires...
"The grain of a benevolent person [is not used] to slaughter living beings for the ancestral altars and dining tables, thereby burdening their parents with many karmic obstacles of rebirth.
How can you be so unbenevolent?
The guest asked: "When descendants perform sacrifices, do the ancestors come to partake of them, or do they not?"

The answer is: According to the *Madhyama Āgama*, if one’s ancestors have been reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), their descendants can cause them to come and partake [of offerings] through sincere devotion.
If they are in the heavenly realms (*deva*), they do not deign to come and partake because they are experiencing bliss.

If they are in the three miserable paths (*durgati*), they cannot come and partake because they are undergoing suffering. If they have been reborn in the human realm (*manuṣya*), they have their own separate relatives and no longer come.
Regarding the ancestral sacrifice: as descendants, you need only ensure that your intentions are sincere and that you treat the ritual with reverence.
Do not indulge in excessive killing to compound the transgressions of the deceased, and do not neglect the fasts that would disturb the mind during the rite of presence. This will suffice;
there is no need to inquire whether the ancestors actually partake of the offerings.
The guest said: "Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty used flour to make sacrificial offerings. Historians argue that this was an omen that [the state] would no longer receive blood sacrifices.
Thus we know that using vegetarian offerings first for sacrifices is contrary to ritual."
The answer is: "The faults of men lie within their respective parties; by observing their faults, their benevolence (*ren*) can be known.
When Emperor Wu of Liang executed the six nobles and flooded the city of Shouyang, this was his lack of benevolence.

However, if we judge it by the use of flour offerings instead of living victims, then from the perspective of the spirits, he avoided the transgression of requiring blood sacrifices, and from the perspective of sentient beings, they obtained the blessing of preserving their lives. This is precisely his benevolence. As for the world at large...

This failure was simply due to the course of national destiny. If it were because of using flour as a sacrificial victim, then how could the rulers of the Chen and Sui dynasties not have used the "great ox" (the three types of sacrificial animals)?
Why did their fall come so swiftly? Master Huiyuan said: "The one who first made the wooden puppet for burial treated it as a human being."

Confucius condemned such persons as being without posterity, so that one must use a sacrificial animal as a substitute for their image when performing sacrifices. Even a benevolent person could not fully satisfy the ancestral spirits with this;

yet to insist on discarding the likeness to employ the actual person—how can that be so heartless? According to historical records, after Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty ascended the throne, he prohibited alcohol and banned meat.

He allowed the people to rest and the armies to cease their labors; his reign was repeatedly recorded as one of great prosperity (*da you*). From the Jin to the Sui dynasties, none who could be called "moderately well-governed" (*xiao kang*) surpassed Emperor Wu of Liang.
He enjoyed the throne for forty-nine years and lived to the age of eighty-six. Later, his descendants served in the Tang dynasty, with eight generations producing prime ministers (*xiang zhai*).
Yet the court historians, because he had devoted himself to Buddhism, suppressed his merits and disparaged him at will. How can this be considered "praising the good" (*shan shan cong zai*)?
The Master’s intention was this:
to resolve the guest’s doubt regarding the departure from custom during a banquet.

The guest said, "When kinsmen and friends are seated together, a vegetarian meal cannot bring true joy; when one is invited by superior companions, it is only with choice delicacies that [the occasion is fulfilled]."
This sufficiently clarifies the matter of ritual propriety. To abolish banquets and feasts out of a desire to protect living beings is not a comprehensive argument.
I reply: If such a person were a virtuous gentleman, they would surely rejoice in my abstention from killing and would not harbor resentment toward my [apparent] negligence.
If that person were jealous of my arrogance, they would surely be a petty man who nourishes only his mouth and body; there would be nothing wrong with being arrogant toward such a person.
Yet, to incur grave offenses for the sake of feeding the mouths of others—I shall not do this.
Formerly, when Su Dongpo entertained guests at Qitong, he presented a poem to Chen Jichang, saying: "I pity the crab in the basket, opening its mouth to guard its remaining juices. Furthermore...
Pity those fish in the basket; with mouths agape, they spit out their last moisture. To have their entrails carved out would cause mutual agony; what more could I possibly gain?

When we meet, we have not yet exchanged pleasantries, yet this is the most urgent matter for which we should exhort one another. Have you not seen Lu Huai-shen? His steaming cauldron resembled a steamed duck;
the guests all suppressed their laughter until he shorn away the lid. Have you not seen Wang Wuzi? At every meal, his knife-block was stained red. [The glass]...
Li Zai offered steamed piglets; within them was human milk, white as snow. Lu Gongxin was truly cold and humble; with his thinning hair, he could barely fit a full cap.
Although Wu Zi’s deeds were grand and noble, before he died, his spirit wept first. You, Master, possess ten-thousand pieces of gold and jade, yet you protect this single flaw like an ant.
A single year forms one dream; a hundred years are but a true traveler passing by. Do not let this poem fall into neglect; let Yan’s verses be compiled into the Du Ji. Indeed.
Since even when hosting a banquet, Dongpo was so earnestly and repeatedly admonishing against killing, why do you harbor doubts regarding the violation of custom in entertaining guests?
This concludes the second inquiry on the doubt concerning killing in the teachings of the ancient sages.
The guest said, "Fuxi fashioned nets and traps for hunting and fishing; was he not, then, [a proponent of killing]?
I replied, "In the age of primordial chaos, birds and beasts multiplied, and if no means were taken to restrain them, humans would have suffered their harm.
Fuxi perhaps taught the people how to defend themselves against them, yet he did not explicitly state that they should eat them. If one were to claim he taught the people to take life, I fear..."
Fishermen and boatmen are often considered reckless, yet they were all ministers of merit to Fuxi; for he untied the nets and released the birds, and presented fish for him to raise.
By comparison, the offenses of various sages and worthies are not so slight.
The guest said: "Confucius cautioned against killing; it was merely that he did not fish without a net and did not shoot at birds roosting overnight.
He never abandoned fishing and hunting altogether. If he had prohibited them entirely, would Confucius not be a model to follow?"
The answer is: This is merely an extreme expression of the Sage’s benevolence in cherishing all things. To discuss it according to the literary conventions of historical records:
the "fisherman" is one who draws in those that were not caught in nets; the "fowler" is one who draws in those that were not shot while roosting.

It does not mean that the Sage truly engaged in fishing or fowling. If one were to claim that he fished and fowled for the sake of nourishment and sacrifice, how could this be compared to Confucius eating coarse grain?
"The custom of drinking water is not true happiness. Is the sacrifice of simple vegetables and vegetable soup then entirely empty talk? How extreme this is!
Those who attempt to fathom the Sage are likewise shallow."
Resolving Doubts Regarding Loving the People and Cherishing All Things (Part Two, Question Two).
A guest said: "The gentleman loves his kin and extends benevolence to the people; he extends benevolence to the people and cherishes all things. These applications follow a sequential order.
To strictly prohibit killing and promote the release of living beings is merely to attend to the secondary."
The answer is: What Mencius spoke of refers to the sequence of intimacy and distance, not the sequence of chronological priority.

If one were required to exhaustively fulfill this [duty to kin] before attending to that [duty to others], then a child who lost his parents at a young age but aspired to benevolence toward the people, or one who had not yet served his sovereign but felt compassion for all creatures, would instead incur the offense of failing his ruler and father.
How could Mencius have made such a restrictive argument?
The guest asked again. He replied:
"It is precisely for the sake of benevolence toward the people that I urge others to love all things. Your love for people is merely for the sake of your own mouth and belly."
Benevolence toward the people is the lesser form of love. My love for others is by way of the mind and will; this is the greater form of benevolence toward the people.
To resolve doubts regarding the distinctions of cause and effect (the six questions) so that they do not become confused:
the mind must be profoundly still (*jijik*). When it is still, thoughts of good and evil do not arise. The mind must be alertly aware (*shōshō*).
When one is alert and aware, no recollection arises; since there is no thought outside the Buddha, one is constantly in a state of profound stillness.
Since the Buddha is within thought, one is constantly alert and aware.
Do not dwell upon the name.
"Not abiding" is precisely contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Contemplation is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The first phrase belongs to the past; the last phrase belongs to the future. The middle phrase also does not abide: the first phrase belongs to the past;
the last phrase belongs to the future. Even the present phrase does not abide. It is perfectly clear and distinct, yet it cannot [be grasped].
To attain and yet not to attain, with absolute clarity and distinction—
whether one holds the name of the Buddha or contemplates a *huatou*,
this is called "investigating Chan" (*chán*). Or, whether one sits and quiets the thoughts, this is called "sitting" (*zuò*).
Chan is *can* (to investigate); it is *zuo* (to sit). All of this is Chan. Chan is Buddha; all of this is mind.
Chan is the Chan of the Buddha, and the Buddha is the Buddha of Chan. How could the Dharma-gate of reciting the Buddha's name hinder the practice of investigating and sitting in Chan?
Furthermore, one who investigates Chan can take these four characters, "A-mi-tuo-fo" (Amitābha Buddha), as a single phrase.
Recite the Buddha’s name again and again, repeating it without ceasing; do not say you are practicing *chan* (meditation), for *chan* is already present therein.

As for those who practice sitting *chan*, they must reach the point where a single thought accords with reality (*yixin xiangying*), suddenly becoming as if suspended in emptiness—only then will they have attained the Way.
When one recites the Buddha’s name until the mind is undisturbed by a single thought, is this not accord? When one recites until the mind is empty, is this not eternal?

It is in accord with this. At the time of mindfulness of the Buddha, when one is neither dull nor distracted, stillness and contemplation, concentration and wisdom, are perfected in every thought-moment.
If you wish to seek dhyāna elsewhere, where else could that dhyāna possibly be?
The precepts are themselves the Buddha; to uphold the name is to uphold the Buddha’s precepts.
Upholding the precepts governs the body; upholding the Buddha’s name governs the mind. Through long-term practice, the mind becomes pure;
through long-term practice, the mind becomes empty. The nature of mindfulness and the nature of the precepts are not two; they are one and the same in every instance of upholding the precepts.

One must not let the head emerge from the mouth of the board. Recite the Buddha’s name with every beat; then, at the moment of death, one will break through the barrier of the ghosts and leap out of the three realms.
If you have already maintained the precepts and possess spiritual practice, dedicate these merits toward the Western Pure Land, and you will certainly be reborn in the middle grade.
If you are unable to attend to both, then diligently recite the Buddha’s name as if your own hair were on fire.

The teachings themselves are the Buddha, and upholding their names constitutes the entire Great Canon. All arise from the mind; if there were no Buddha within the mind, the teachings would likewise be in vain.

Yet, who among those with minds does not possess a Buddha? It is simply that they do not think of it themselves. Among those following the teachings, there is none who has not read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Indeed, among those who study the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there is not one who does not hold Śrāvakasīta lightly while regarding Avalokiteśvara with great reverence.

Yet this very view has already become the root of birth and death. Even if you manage to acquire various kinds of knowledge and abilities, they will do nothing more than nourish the sprouts of suffering;

at the critical juncture of birth and death, they will prove utterly ineffective. I pray that you will quickly let go of all attachments, be reborn in the Western Land, and personally behold the Buddha.
Maitreya. If you are unable to let go [of attachments], then dedicate the merit of studying and expounding this scripture toward the Western Land and make the Four Great Vows;

thus it shall not be in vain. If you propagate the single gate of the Pure Land and explain in detail the merits of *nien-fo*, then every glance and every thought will be an adornment of the Western Land, leading to rebirth in the highest grade. Furthermore—
Furthermore, what is there to doubt?

One has not yet finished performing a single act of upholding [the precepts], nor has one even concluded a single utterance, and one has not yet prepared oneself for mindfulness of the Buddha; yet, the four-character name of the Buddha—
It gushes forth in rolling waves. This is a sign that this samādhi is easily accomplished.
To "hold" yet not "hold" means to hold it without slackening.
"Sufficiently swift" and "again sufficiently swift" refers to clearly and distinctly holding these four characters at the time of reciting the Buddha’s name.

When the discursive thoughts do not shift and the four characters suddenly come to a halt, there is neither a thought that clings to the four characters, nor a thought that is separate from the four characters, nor a thought outside of the four characters.

This is called a temporary attainment of a superior state; it is not yet the true emptiness of the mind. However, if one recites the Buddha’s name with diligent persistence, this state will appear repeatedly. Then...
Gradually the mind becomes empty. If, because of a single thought the mind becomes empty and one consequently pursues dullness and torpor, this is called a lack of wisdom.
One should know that as the mind becomes increasingly empty, mindfulness becomes increasingly alert; as the mind becomes increasingly empty, mindfulness becomes increasingly pure.

Within the Buddha-mind, where is the "self" that conceives of self, and where is the Buddha within the mind? As for emptiness and non-emptiness, where else could they possibly reside? It is like the sun.
Together with the moon, its brilliance blazing forth, it ascends a precious palace and circumambulates Mount Sumeru, flowing everywhere to illuminate the world below.
Alas! How wondrous is this perfect and luminous enlightenment!

A solitary bhikṣu upholding the Name cultivates the Way without seeking companionship. In the realm of mindfulness of the Buddha, solitude is most excellent. Whether in high or low circumstances, there is what is appropriate;
whether slow or swift, one acts according to one's capacity. To achieve a state of unified integration—this is precisely the time for it. One should know that while the body is solitary, the mind...
One is not alone. The hearts of all Buddhas and Amitābha have never for a moment abandoned me. When I raise a thought, the Buddha knows it;
when I open my mouth, the Buddha hears it. Why worry about being lonely and isolated? This is so even if one has not yet fully mastered the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.

One should purchase many Pure Land texts and read them—such as the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Contemplation Sūtra*, Master Zhiyi’s *Treatise on the Ten Doubts*, and Chan Master Tianru Ze’s *Questions on the Pure Land*.

One should diligently study such works as *Master Dayou’s Guide to the Pure Land*, *Longshu’s Text on the Pure Land*, *The Morning Bell of the Pure Land*, *The Passport to the West*, *A Precise Pointer to the West*, *The Yunqi Collection*, and the *Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*.

These have been mentioned here merely as examples that are clear and easy to understand; beyond these, there are many other excellent texts that could not possibly be listed in full. Furthermore, one should seek out those who are thoroughly versed in the Pure Land teachings and consult them.
Question: "The period for observing the precepts and reciting the name results in meager merit.
Answer: "Eating meat is your official duty; abstaining from it is your blessing. Observing the fast and refraining from killing is precisely the accumulation of merit."
[The Master] said, "I have heard that one who eats meat must fast for three days. How could eight mouths alone be called 'merit'?
The guest said, "If I believe these words, I must certainly observe the fast before it is permissible. I do not know whether Confucius also observed such fasts."
The answer is: The *Book of Documents* states, "In fasting, one must change one's food. It also says, "That which you, my son, must be careful about is fasting.
The *Book of Rites* speaks of "internal fasting" (*caizhai*) and "external fasting" (*sanzhai*). These instances can be examined one by one.
Now, if people cannot follow Confucius in every matter, yet alone use the eating of meat as an excuse to claim they follow him—is it that Confucius himself was still a vulgar person who ate meat?
The guest said, “It is certainly good to observe the fast, but what of it that one’s physical appearance has become so withered and emaciated?
How can this be endured? He replied, “The true self is of primary importance; the provisional body is of secondary significance.

Furthermore, when the divine spirits mete out rewards and punishments, do they judge a person by their physical appearance, or do they judge them by the workings of their heart and mind? You have simply failed to reflect upon this.”
The guest asked: "Regarding the five kinds of pungent plants that grow in their own native lands, why does the Buddhist scripture prohibit them all together?

He replied: "The sutra states that it is because they are pungent and foul-smelling, because they can obstruct bodhi, and because the devas loathe and reject them. When [the guest] asked about the ripening [of their karma], [he replied:]...
"Eating aids lust; eating raw food arouses anger. Thus, malevolent spirits and hungry ghosts often smell the breath from one's lips.
The guest asked, "Some say that although I do not observe the fast, it is still better than observing it and then breaking it.
Others say that although I observe the fast and break it, it is still better than not observing it at all. What do you think?"
The answer is: For example, it is like holding a government office. Those who do not observe the fast are like those who have never entered public service.
Those who observe it but then break it are like those who have already entered service but were subsequently dismissed. Which is superior and which is inferior?
The guest said, "I also wish to observe the fast, yet when delicious flavors appear before me, I cannot control myself. What can be done?
He replied, "A person of superior capacity arouses immeasurable compassion and simply cannot bear to eat. Otherwise, one should regard [the food] as the five kinds of impurity."
If one maintains such reflections, one will certainly be able to observe the fast. First, that seed is impure; second, that which is eaten is impure;
third, that dwelling place is impure; fourth, that belly is impure; fifth, that which follows after death is impure.
If one constantly maintains these reflections, how could one fail to observe the fast?
Explaining the Doubt Regarding the Difficulty of Believing in the Buddha’s Principle (Three Questions).

A guest asked: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rescue those in suffering by seeking their cries. Yet Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty served the Buddha, and subsequently starved to death at Taicheng. Why was this?"

The reply states: "Starving to death in the Tai City—this is the talk of pedantic Confucians. The *Tongjian* records that when Hou Jing attacked and captured the Tai City, he saw Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty;
his countenance remained unchanged, and [Hou Jing] did not dare look up at him. He withdrew and informed Wang Senggui, saying, "His heavenly majesty is difficult to offend;
I do not dare see him again. Later, Wang Lun presented several hundred eggs to Emperor Wu. [Emperor Wu]...
His mouth was bitter. He asked for honey but received none; he uttered "he-he" twice and then passed away. His husband said, "If his mouth was bitter, it can be known that his stomach was not empty.
If he sought honey, it can be known that he was not seeking to cure hunger. Furthermore, since there were several hundred eggs, other provisions must have been equal in number.
How could there be any reason for him to die of starvation? Alas! Those who read history throughout the world often praise [him] as uniquely endowed..."
Only this single passage from the historical record serves as my sole eye; I have unwittingly substituted my ears for my eyes—how profound is the depth of such habitual conditioning!
A guest said: "Later commentators all claim that when Emperor Wu 'sacrificed his body,' he sacrificed it along with his entire empire. I—"
For this reason, I do not accept it.

He replied: "From antiquity to the present, among both sages and ordinary people, there has never been one who did not discard their body. Take yourself, for instance; today you [regard it] deeply as..."
The two characters "A" and "Ye. I do not know where they have gone. How excellent is this diligence amidst illness!

At the time of death, when holding the Name, simply remember these four characters: "A-mi-tuo-fo. Do not forget them. If you can recite them loudly, then recite them loudly. If you can recite them high, then recite them high.
Lower the mind slightly. Then lower it again. If one is unable to do so whether high or low, one should likewise silently keep these four characters in mind so as not to forget them.
Those attending on the left and right should also constantly remind [the practitioner] of these four characters repeatedly.
One should know that all the paths of wandering through hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes are entirely contained within this moment.
A single thought can decisively determine one’s destiny. Why is this? The cycle of the six realms of rebirth is governed entirely by a single thought.
If one directs that single thought with focused concentration toward the Buddha, then even though the physical form may perish, the spirit will not be scattered;
thus, following that very thought, one shall be reborn in the Pure Land. Alas! Simply keep in mind these four characters: *Āmítuófó*. Do not...
It is forgetfulness.
Alas! To make vows, repent, and hold fast to the Name—how many in this world are ignorant of the practice of nianfo! Among the Confucians, there are those who cast out the Buddha as a heretic.
Yet they are unwilling to practice mindfulness. Those who have left the household life treat mindfulness of the Buddha as a mere routine, failing to understand the reason for such mindfulness.
Those with wild wisdom know that a Buddha exists but disdain to practice mindfulness; those who are ignorant do not even know of the Buddha and thus cannot practice mindfulness.
This is the general rule. Even among the rustic and simple folk, when they hear the teaching on cause and effect, they too know to practice mindfulness.
Even those who recite the Buddha’s name while still yearning for a future life to receive karmic rewards remain, as before, sowing the seeds of saṃsāra.
Among those who seek to recite the Buddha’s name solely for the purpose of ending birth and death, there is perhaps only one or two in a hundred.

One must know that once a person has begun to recite the Buddha’s name, they should take the Buddha’s mind as their own mind, cultivate the Buddha’s compassion, and give rise to vast vows to deliver and save all beings.
For all sentient beings, I universally repent for all defilements, grudges, and entanglements. All merits, great and small, I dedicate toward the Western Land.
In this way, one possesses the true cause for the practice of Buddha-recollection.
